posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a glossy chestnut mare with a flaxen mane and gold earring standing in an indoor arena doorway with a smug side glance. Text at the top reads: I was early to the arena, so I stood behind the door for ten minutes to arrive late. That's called an entrance.
posts.caption: I've watched her do this at every show since spring. She checks the clock, checks the door, and decides she's early. Then she waits by the trailer with her ears forward like she's been given a secret. Last month the in-gate steward held the next class a full minute because she assumed the horse had a schedule. She does. It just doesn't involve anyone else. I braided her forelock at 6:30 and by eight she'd rearranged it to suit herself. We came in third. She took the ribbon like she'd been told to expect it.
posts.first: At the last show I found her standing exactly where I'd left her, facing the arena, dead still. I'd tied her to the trailer an hour earlier and she hadn't touched her hay bag. When I asked what she was doing she flicked one ear. I took that to mean timing.

posts.caption: The tarp came off the hay stack last week in a gust that sounded like applause. Pudding was at the far fence before the second flap. I found him behind the water trough with straw in his forelock, staring at the barn like it owed him money. It took four carrots and a lot of quiet talking to get him to look at it again. He did, with one eye, turning his whole body so the other one didn't have to. The tarp now has six bungees and two cinder blocks on it.
posts.first: I put the tarp back on that evening, weighed down with a bucket for good measure. Pudding watched from the gate the whole time. When I finished he walked up, sniffed the bucket, and went to bed. I assume we both feel better about it. I've never asked.

posts.quote: I fell off at a walk, in front of the vet, into fresh shavings. The horse waited until I stood up to look embarrassed.
posts.first: I still have the shavings stain on my good jeans. The vet was kind enough to look at the horse's teeth for ten minutes. The horse kept his face carefully blank the whole time. We've never discussed it, but he watched the trailer very closely for the rest of the day.

posts.caption: He was a fast horse once. There's a barn photo to prove it, a gray blur from a spring morning in 2009. These days he does his rounds at the pace of a man reading the paper. He stops at the water trough, then the fence post, then the exact patch of sun by the hay shed. Nothing he does is rushed and nothing gets missed. The young mare in the next paddock watches him with real respect. She's trying to work out where he's going. He's already there.
posts.first: I hung his old halter on a nail by the feed room last spring. It hangs a little low now and looks sad. He walked past it twice today and didn't seem to notice. I notice it every time. It doesn't seem to bother him that I do.

Headline: A coworker asked why my horse can't just eat the lawn. Subtitle: I showed her the hay bill. She offered her lawn.
posts.caption: Bales were $9 each when I started this and I've lost track of the number since. I keep the receipts in a coffee can in the tack room, and the can is full. Last month a woman from my office asked what the horse eats in winter. I said hay, about forty pounds a day. She asked whether I'd tried less. Red watched this conversation from the fence with the stillness of a mare who has done the math. The woman now says good morning to the can.
posts.first: Red eats before I do every day, and she knows it. At six, in the dark, she's at the gate, waiting for the sound of the hay door. I bring her breakfast, then the thermos goes down on a bale. It's the only quiet half hour I get all day. She doesn't share it with anyone.

posts.caption: Her steps have changed since September. She goes down the barn stairs sideways now, one hand on the rail, and insists they got taller. I've stopped mentioning it because it only makes her put on the face. The heating pad hangs on a hook in the tack room next to the bridles, where it has apparently lived all year. Every morning she brings the good carrots and a warm mash and talks to me about nothing. I keep very still when she climbs on. We've never discussed any of it, and I'd like to keep it that way.
posts.first: She keeps the mounting block next to my stall so she doesn't have to explain it to anyone. It used to live by the arena. One morning in October it moved, quietly. I walked over, stood beside it, and let her think it was her idea.
